prompt:

   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?

   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?

   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?

   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?

   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?

   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?

   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Uber shows several Rule Breaker traits: it is the top dog in global app-based mobility, has a household-name brand and a sustainable advantage from its two-sided network, and is backed by notable investors such as Pershing Square. It misses on price momentum (shares down about 26% over 52 weeks to $70.35) and is no longer a young, emerging company, so the fit is good but not ideal.
summaries.buffett: Uber now earns real money (2025 operating income $5.6 billion, free cash flow $9.8 billion) and buys back shares, but it has only been profitable for about three years, carries more debt ($12.7 billion) than cash ($5.4 billion), and has a moat that robotaxis could disrupt. A Buffett-style investor would find the long record of consistent earnings and predictable economics missing.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the network effects and the cultural turnaround since 2017, but inverting raises clear failure paths: driverless fleets bypassing Uber, regulation of gig drivers and heavily funded Chinese rivals. The business is understandable, yet it is not the kind of simple, durably dominant franchise he favoured.
summaries.lynch: Uber fits Lynch's fast-grower category with a simple story: more trips, more Uber One members and expanding delivery, with Gross Bookings up 24% in Q2 2026. Its PEG of about 0.6 on forward non-GAAP earnings and shrinking share count are attractive, though it is heavily followed by Wall Street and insiders are not buying.
summaries.fisher: Uber keeps launching new products (Uber One, grocery and retail delivery, advertising, AV partnerships) and is unusually strong at selling through a single global app. Margins have improved sharply, but its R&D now mostly refines the marketplace rather than creating new technology, and labour relations with drivers remain a weak point.
summaries.graham: Uber fails most of Graham's defensive-investor tests: it pays no dividend, has not been profitable for ten years, trades at about 21 times its three-year average EPS and around 80 times on P/E x P/B, and its current ratio is close to 1. It is not a Graham-style stock.
summaries.thiel: Uber was a classic Zero to One company that started with black cars in San Francisco and expanded worldwide with superb distribution, but today it faces many competitors and its technology is not ten times better than rivals'. Its future depends on whether it becomes the main aggregator for autonomous vehicles, which is not assured.
summaries.gerstner: Uber matches Gerstner's focus on durable growth with discipline: Gross Bookings are compounding around 20%, free cash flow passed $10 billion over the trailing year, and the company is cutting its share count. The stock's derating on autonomous-vehicle fears creates a debate on whether the market is mispricing it as a robotaxi loser rather than the leading AV demand platform.
summaries.druckenmiller: Earnings are rising quickly (non-GAAP EPS up 35% in Q2 2026) and there are catalysts such as AV launches and the Delivery Hero deal, but the stock has trended down for a year and the narrative is clouded by robotaxi competition. Druckenmiller typically wants price action and estimate revisions to confirm a thesis, which are currently missing.
summaries.smith: Uber's 39.8% gross margin, 10.7% operating margin and debt-funded acquisitions fall short of Terry Smith's standard of high returns on capital with high, stable margins. Its strong free cash flow and network effects are positives, but it does not yet look like a Fundsmith-style compounder.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Uber's earnings yield (trailing operating income about $6.7 billion on an enterprise value near $151 billion, about 4.4%) is modest, while return on capital is decent at around 19%. It would not rank near the top of a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Uber has a good business with growing free cash flow and a management team that has executed well, but Akre's three-legged stool also asks for high, consistent returns and a long reinvestment runway at those returns; Uber's AV spending (more than $10 billion planned) and the $14.8 billion Delivery Hero bid make the reinvestment returns uncertain.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for low-risk, high-uncertainty bets on simple, existing businesses at deep discounts. Uber is cheaper after its fall (about 7% free cash flow yield) and the AV worry is a recognisable uncertainty, but the downside is not clearly limited and the stock is not trading at a large discount to conservative value.
summaries.wood: Uber touches ARK's autonomous mobility theme as a ride platform that partners with Waymo, Wayve, Baidu and others, but ARK has argued that vertically integrated robotaxi players like Tesla will capture most of the value. Uber is a beneficiary of the robotaxi platform shift only if it remains the demand aggregator.
summaries.ackman: Uber fits Pershing Square's criteria closely enough that Ackman made it a top holding (about 30 million shares, roughly 15.7% of the portfolio as of the latest 13F): a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative platform with a dominant market position and a share price he judged below intrinsic value. The risk is that autonomy changes the industry's economics.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model fits partly: Uber passes some scale benefits to users through Uber One discounts and better driver density, but it has been raising take rates and cutting incentives rather than steadily lowering prices. Its position in 10-20 years depends on the uncertain outcome of autonomy.
summaries.valentine: Uber solves a large, painful problem (getting a reliable ride or meal quickly) for hundreds of millions of people, which Valentine would value. As a 17-year-old, $144 billion public company it is far beyond the early-stage, big-market venture bets he made at Sequoia.
summaries.nash: Uber passes several of Nash's tests: it rides big trends (urban mobility, delivery and autonomy), revenue grows above 10%, it is profitable with strong free cash flow and a forward PEG near 0.6. It fails his instant kills of more debt than cash and an operating margin below 20%, and scores about 70 of 130 on his 13 categories, below the 75 threshold.

momentum.evidence: The share price was $70.35 on October 16, 2026, down about 26% over 52 weeks and near the low end of its $65.41-$100.35 range.

g4.evidence: CEO Dara Khosrowshahi turned Uber from a $4.9 billion operating loss in 2020 to $5.6 billion profit in 2025, and Pershing Square holds about 30 million shares, roughly 15.7% of its portfolio.

g6.evidence: Bears argue robotaxis make Uber's model obsolete, but most commentators now call it cheap: forward P/E about 17, PEG about 0.6, and 41 of 50 analysts rate it Buy with an average target of $100.86.

simple.evidence: Uber takes a cut of rides, deliveries and freight loads booked on its apps, a model a careful generalist can follow through Gross Bookings, take rate and margin.

b2.evidence: Uber lost money every year until 2022 (net loss $9.1 billion in 2022) and only became consistently profitable on an operating basis from 2023.

integrity.evidence: Management has been candid and disciplined since 2017, repurchasing $6.5 billion of stock in 2025, but stock-based compensation remains large ($1.8 billion in 2025) and insiders own only about 0.2%.

b6.evidence: Uber avoided building its own self-driving cars (selling ATG to Aurora in 2020), but the $14.8 billion all-cash Delivery Hero bid and other acquisitions ($647 million in Q2 2026) show an appetite for big deals.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 19% on trailing figures, but it has only recently turned positive and is inflated by tax benefits and equity revaluations.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $9.8 billion in 2025 (18.8% of revenue), above GAAP operating income of $5.6 billion, and passed $10 billion on a trailing basis in Q2 2026.

b10.evidence: Uber still carries a large accumulated deficit from years of losses, so there are no retained earnings to judge, although its market value (about $144 billion) is well above the capital raised in its 2019 IPO.

safety.evidence: A Nash-style DCF at a 12% discount rate with growth trimmed to 15% gives about $71 per share, close to the $70.35 price, so there is no wide margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: At about 17 times forward earnings with non-GAAP EPS expected to grow about 37% in 2026 and a 7% free-cash-flow yield, the price looks reasonable for the growth.

mu5.evidence: Several failure paths exist: robotaxi operators such as Waymo and Tesla bypassing Uber, gig-worker reclassification, heavily funded Chinese rivals in Brazil and debt from the Delivery Hero takeover.

reinvest.evidence: Uber can reinvest in delivery expansion, advertising and AV partnerships (more than $10 billion planned for AVs), but the returns on those investments are unproven.

ly2.evidence: It is a fast grower with a simple story: Gross Bookings up 24% to $58.0 billion in Q2 2026 as more people use rides, delivery and Uber One.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 15 and forward P/E of about 17 are below the roughly 37% expected 2026 non-GAAP EPS growth (PEG about 0.6).

runway.evidence: Analysts expect revenue to grow from $52.0 billion in 2025 to about $88.9 billion in 2030, and Uber is expanding into groceries, ads, robotaxis and, via Delivery Hero, new regions.

ly7.evidence: Weighted diluted shares fell from 2,150.5 million in 2024 to 2,050.2 million in Q2 2026 thanks to buybacks, but insiders are not buying shares in the open market.

ly8.evidence: Uber is covered by about 50 analysts and is one of the most discussed stocks on Wall Street.

fi2.evidence: Uber keeps adding products such as Uber One (50 million members), grocery and retail delivery, Journey Ads and robotaxi rides with partners like Waymo and Wayve.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $3.4 billion in 2025 supports a fast-improving marketplace and new features, but it has not produced proprietary breakthrough technology like self-driving.

fi4.evidence: Uber's single global app and Uber One membership drove record first-time users in Q2 2026 and 208 million monthly active consumers.

longterm.evidence: Management is investing for the long term in AVs and the Delivery Hero deal, while also prioritising near-term profit growth and large buybacks.

gr1.evidence: Uber had $52.0 billion of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $144 billion.

ni10.evidence: Uber reported net losses in 2020, 2021 and 2022 (2022 net loss $9,141 million).

gr4.evidence: Uber has never paid a dividend.

eps10.evidence: Uber did not have positive EPS ten years ago; diluted EPS was -$3.86 in 2020, so the ten-year test cannot be met.

gr6.evidence: Average diluted EPS over 2023-2025 was about $3.39 ($0.87, $4.56, $4.73), so the price is about 21 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 15.4 times P/B of about 5.3 is roughly 80, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Uber's app and matching technology are good but not ten times better than Lyft, DoorDash, Bolt or DiDi.

timing.evidence: Demand for app-based rides and delivery is still growing about 20%, but the arrival of robotaxis makes this a pivotal moment that could help or hurt Uber.

th3.evidence: Uber began with black-car rides in San Francisco in 2010 and expanded to over 70 countries and into delivery and freight.

th5.evidence: Its app reaches 208 million monthly active consumers, giving it the distribution that AV partners such as Waymo, Wayve and Baidu tap into.

durable.evidence: Network effects are strong today, but Waymo is ending its exclusive Uber deals in Austin and Atlanta by early 2028 and robotaxi fleets could weaken Uber's position in 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Uber's opportunity is now well understood and contested by many rivals; its AV aggregator strategy is also pursued by Lyft and others.

trend.evidence: Uber aims to be the largest platform for autonomous vehicle rides, but it does not own the AI driving technology at the heart of the shift.

dr1.evidence: Non-GAAP EPS grew 44% in Q1 2026 and 35% in Q2 2026, but the Q3 2026 profit guidance came in below analysts' expectations.

dr2.evidence: Robotaxi launches with partners in London and US cities and the Delivery Hero deal could improve the picture, but the outcome of AV competition is uncertain.

dr4.evidence: Consumer spending on rides and food is sensitive to the economy and fuel prices, and lower rates would ease the cost of the debt-funded Delivery Hero deal.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming catalysts include Q3 2026 results, AV launches such as the Wayve robotaxi trial in London, ongoing buybacks and the expected 2H 2027 close of the Delivery Hero takeover.

dr7.evidence: Pershing Square holds about 15.7% of its portfolio in Uber, but the AV debate makes it a contested, not consensus, high-conviction idea.

gm.evidence: Reported gross margin (revenue less cost of revenue) was 39.8% in 2025, down from 53.7% in 2020 because of business model changes, so it is moderate rather than high.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $10.1 billion on a market value of about $144 billion is a free-cash-flow yield of about 7%.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $6.7 billion against an enterprise value of about $151 billion is an earnings yield of only about 4.4%.

pa2.evidence: The stock fell about 26% in a year on AV fears and Brazil competition while bookings kept growing over 20%, but the AV threat may not be temporary.

pa4.evidence: Strong free cash flow and a dominant network limit downside, but debt exceeds cash and robotaxi disruption could permanently impair the business.

wo1.evidence: Uber is a major robotaxi distribution platform with partners such as Waymo, Wayve and Baidu, but it does not develop autonomous driving technology itself.

wo2.evidence: Uber's costs depend mainly on driver pay, which does not fall quickly with volume; only robotaxis could sharply cut costs, and those belong to its partners.

wo3.evidence: Uber touches autonomous mobility but does not combine several of ARK's platforms such as AI, robotics, energy storage or blockchain.

wo4.evidence: Analysts expect revenue to grow about 11% a year to roughly $88.9 billion in 2030, far from a many-fold increase in five years.

ac3.evidence: Uber owns no vehicles, but fuel prices affect driver supply, consumer spending drives demand and currency moves affect reported results.

ns1.evidence: Uber One discounts and denser networks pass some benefits to users, but Uber has also raised take rates and fees as it grew.

ns4.evidence: Uber's position in 10-20 years depends on whether robotaxi makers sell rides through its app or their own, which is still unresolved.

va2.evidence: Uber solves the everyday pain of getting a reliable ride or meal fast, across 13.6 billion trips in 2025.

tn1.evidence: Uber was built for the app-based mobility trend and positions itself as the AV demand platform, but it is not the infrastructure layer of autonomy.

tn2.evidence: The market prices Uber as a possible robotaxi loser, while management argues it is becoming the largest platform for autonomous vehicle rides; which story wins is unclear.

tn3.evidence: Uber is a large-cap US company, not Chinese, not a commodity producer or airline, and was founded in 2009.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year from 2020 to 2025 and Uber is profitable, though debt ($12.7 billion) exceeds cash ($5.4 billion), passing two of three.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in each of the last six quarters (e.g. $2.3 billion in Q1 and $2.8 billion in Q2 2026), but debt exceeded cash every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 18% in 2025 and 12% in Q2 2026, with consensus at about 11% for 2026 despite business model changes cutting reported growth by 8-9 points.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 18.3% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 18.8% is about 37, below 40, and lower on trailing figures.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue grew 18.3% while total costs and expenses grew 12.8%, and trailing operating income kept rising in 2026.

tn9.evidence: It fails two instant kills: debt of $12.7 billion exceeds cash of $5.4 billion, and the 2025 operating margin was 10.7%, below 20%.

tn10.evidence: Uber faces driver classification rules and over 150,000 US driver arbitration demands, and its Delivery Hero takeover needs merger and regulatory clearances.

tn11.evidence: Uber provides an app that helps people get rides and deliveries quickly and helps drivers earn, charging a cut of each booking plus membership and ad fees; it wins on network size and reliability.

tn13.evidence: Total about 70: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 5, operating margin 5, short interest 10 (2.4%), institutional ownership 10 (84%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, and 5 each for moat, CEO, pricing power, secular trend, culture and talent.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year and operating margin expanded, but free cash flow was negative in 2020 and 2021 and debt exceeded cash in every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage was strong (2025 operating income $5,565 million vs interest $440 million, about 12.6x) and liabilities were 1.2x equity, but assets excluding goodwill were only about 1.57x liabilities and the latest current ratio is about 0.84.

tn18.evidence: Khosrowshahi has a strong execution record since 2017, but he is not a founder, has under ten years in the role and has not made notable open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Q1 2026 Gross Bookings beat the top of guidance, but Q2 2026 revenue of $14.19 billion missed estimates and Q3 guidance came in below expectations.

tn21.evidence: There is no sign of fraud and no co-CEO, but the $14.8 billion Delivery Hero bid and other acquisitions, a falling reported gross margin and regular insider selling are yellow flags.

tn22.evidence: Uber has $52.0 billion of revenue, about $10 billion of trailing free cash flow and is shrinking its share count, the opposite of a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At $70.35 a 12% discount rate DCF implies about 15% annual revenue growth with a 14.5% FCF margin, roughly in line with recent 17-18% revenue and about 20% Gross Bookings growth, so the margin of comfort is small.

tn25.evidence: Using the 3-year averages (17.7% growth, 14.5% FCF margin) the value is about $79 per share at 12%, but with growth trimmed to 15% it is about $71, roughly equal to the $70.35 price.

tn26.evidence: The forward P/E of about 17 against roughly 37% expected 2026 EPS growth gives a PEG of about 0.6, attractive versus internet platform peers.
